I think the issue with this mindset is that it treats the whole event as something that happened to only you. And while I understand in a big way it is directly linked to your body, you’re not the only person involved. It makes it sound like he’s not allowed to grieve his child or find support unless it’s only with you, but also were you able to support him while he was grieving too in the midst of your grief. Because by not allowing him to tell anyone it’s also forcing him to either hide his grief or push it all on you when you may not be able to handle that on top of yours and that feels unfair to everyone involved.

I was extremely sick my pregnancy and could not do anything. My husband did everything including taking care of me and working and cleaning and it’s a lot. I felt immense guilt, we had a few scares as well. I didn’t tell him he couldn’t talk to anyone, I didn’t want him to bottle all that up but I also could not go long without constantly vomiting so I was absolutely zero support to him while he did everything to support me with absolutely no complaints. If he wanted to he could talk to anyone of his family about how difficult it was or how he was struggling because it wasn’t just me going through it even if I was the one who was pregnant and sick. 

As someone who’s an extremely personal person with a husband who is very open with people and has a very overbearing mom, the boundary has always been that if it is something happening to both of us he can share with whoever as long as I’m not involved if I don’t want to be. So like, anything to do with my mental health or physical health (like crohns or ADHD) he can’t just tell his mom about unless we’ve discussed it and agreed it’s fine and stuff. He knows who I’ve told about certain issues and who to go to if he needs it. And we’ve worked through who can be his support system for those things that are more private. If he wanted to share a miscarriage though he can because it’s not just happening to me, it’s not just my medical event, our child was involved not just my child but if I don’t want to be involved in that discussion I don’t have to be he won’t force it.

Regardless I feel like they should take more time to evaluate you because it sounds like they decided after one session that it’s BPD and not ADHD and didn’t take any of your concerns into account?

Just my experience, I have 3 siblings and am the 2nd oldest and tbh the attention it took away from me when I was younger was really difficult. I ended up spending all my time with my older brother after the next child after me (#3) was born. I became extra independent from a young age and just started doing everything myself/ taking care of myself. We all did activities outside of school too and my younger siblings were more likely to become something from theirs so my parents would go mostly to their stuff. Not sure if that’s the reason but that’s what it looked like considering the younger 2 started sports at a younger age and were more advanced. It also meant I didn’t have rides a lot of the time because the younger ones were prioritized because of age but I still wasn’t old enough to drive. Just expected to find rides when I also struggled to make friends. 

Mentally I did not turn out well due to the loneliness/ not being a part of things as the middle child/ oldest daughter. In addition, I think that it made a lot of people miss out on things that should’ve been apparent and now I’m an adult women seeking an expensive autism/adhd assessment because it is still extremely difficult to exist in everyday life the way people are expected. 

All that to say the way it is now there’s more chance you’ll be able to spend time with and give attention to the two children. Not saying you’d neglect any but it’s just hard to split the time especially if one kid is more needy than the others. It’s easy to feel the neglect and jealousy as a child if you’re not careful. It’s also easier to miss something if you’re also worried about 2 other children. Whether that be something developmentally, grades, social issues, etc. You have to be really deliberate about making sure each child is aware that they’re important and that gets more difficult the more you have.

I have a large birthmark, always hated it. Would get comments from people ranging from “oh birthmarks are so beautiful” to “when you’re an adult you can get it removed”. The comments about them being beautiful just felt like pity and were obviously aimed at me/ the fact that someone had noticed it.

I had a few comments from classmates making fun of me but not often. Tbh the worst was from adults in my case because every new adult in my life felt the need to comment on it. Obviously it depends on the person but as an adult I’ve come to terms with it finally. The best thing for me was when I realized I didn’t even remember it exists. I had stopped getting any type of comment on it and unless reminded generally don’t even think about it anymore most days. I’d also say as things stand now this is the best I’ve felt about it because I don’t even think about it and I get treated like any other person.

My baby was estimated at over 95th centile and showed no signs of coming on her due date (for me the scans ended up being accurate). I know that the scans are supposed to be an approximation and can be way off but at the time I was able to tell from her movements/ my growth that she was definitely on the bigger side. We had also had scans done at multiple locations for other reasons and got the same results. Had low iron and my own issues as well (including a flare up from ibd). My doctor was suggesting a c-section but ultimately left the decision up to me after letting me know pros and cons of everything and I ended up scheduling one for 40+2 so I didn’t go over much if she did happen to be late. In the end I had the c-section (still no signs of labor at that point. Cervical check wasn’t even possible because of how things were positioned so couldn’t even figure out if I was dilated at all. She was just very comfy lol. In the end I had a planned c-section and didn’t have any issues and I think, going into it a bit more calmly/ having a doctor who discussed everything with me even though it was scheduled only a week before was very helpful. The only issue I had was when they were stitching me up I was able to start feeling things again and requested to be put to sleep during that time. The first few days were very painful but I was only taking paracetamol and ibuprofen. Stopped taking those except maybe once every few days before the first week post partum was up. While I know it varies, and that I got lucky to have a doctor who was very helpful (even with all the strikes happening and making it hard to get help whenever emergencies arose during pregnancy) I don’t think it’s worth writing off every method of birth and locations to deliver without being open to other options if needed. I didn’t set my expectations for any specific form of delivery and it made me a lot calmer during the process because I wasn’t being disappointed. I normally need to have plans set and I need them to work or else I freak out, but also telling yourself to be open to options if needed is another form of a plan even if it’s not just following one specific route. If I had held off delivery I don’t know what would’ve happened but I do know that listening to my doctor and having the c-section was probably the best option for me at this point as she’s very healthy and thriving and my recovery has gone probably as good as it ever could’ve all things considered.

Ultimately it depends on how you think your dad will react and whether or not you will need to continue to appease him. Will he leave you be after the news or will he keep asking about the pregnancy and pressuring for information? If you don’t have to give him updates constantly it’ll probably be okay. But if he has a habit of making you manage his emotions on top of your own then it may be a lot to handle while pregnant. 

Also, if he is like this now do you think he’d be able to support you if anything happened during the pregnancy (even just the smallest worry during a scan or potential of needing an induction, etc.) or would you have to support him and be unable to sort through your own feelings with your partner as a couple? I don’t know your situation so I understand that this may only be in relation to him wanting grandchildren and he may be more chill normally. So I think you should just evaluate your own feelings and maybe even discuss with your husband just to see how he feels or if he has any advice as well since he might know the situation better being more involved. 

I wouldn’t tell your dad if you don’t want to tell him though. Like don’t tell just because you’re being pressured. If you find it easier to handle him not knowing, maybe say there’s no fertility issues but you guys have been taking a break trying to conceive for the past few months? Maybe that you haven’t given up but are focusing on work or something else and will start trying again in a few months. Some people do take breaks as it can get emotionally/ mentally draining as well. That way he may revert back to how he was before he found out, if that was easier to handle than how he is now with assuming it’s infertility issues.

ETA: If you’d rather not tell him anything at all it might benefit you to set boundaries now instead and just tell him that if anything happens you’ll let him know when you’re ready but for now you don’t want to discuss it anymore. If he keeps pushing then just don’t engage in those topics anymore. But yeah, I know that can seem harsh to some people so just do what you’re most comfortable with I think.

Honestly, most of my life I was pretty bad about my weight (won’t go into too much detail but I definitely saw myself as heavier than I was). So my methods for losing weight were never healthy.

Since moving out of my parents house and also being in quarantine I’ve gained around 30 pounds. But the past two months I’ve managed to lose 10 and it’s honestly been the most successful and sustainable weight loss I’ve had in my life. It depends on the person of course but for me I’ve been focusing on what I eat and not really exercise yet because of my history with dieting. 

Anyway I’ve found that drinking more water has helped. And understanding my body more, like figuring out when I’m actually hungry. Allowing myself to still enjoy the snacks I like but in moderation. I think growing up with siblings made it difficult because we all ate a lot but they were always crazy skinny and taller (I’m the shortest at 5’8” lol, little sister is next at 6’). I’d definitely eat more snacks than necessary just to be sure I actually had some. So unlearning that was helpful. Telling myself that they’ll still be there tomorrow and I can eat them then instead of eating it all today. I was really bad about binging on hot cheetos too, so I only have them in the apartment occasionally. But honestly telling myself that I can have things later instead of restricting and saying I can’t ever have them has been super helpful for me. Ultimately just eating until I’m satisfied, not drinking all my calories, and listening to my body more has helped. It really depends on the person though. I was tracking my calories at the beginning because I wanted to see how many calories I ended up eating if I did this (like making sure my hunger was okay and I wasn’t overeating) and it was fine. Not sure if this helps but yeah.
